Valley of the Shadow of Death
văl´ĭ ŭv thē shăd´ō ŭv dĕth
n. phrase (the dark ravine of Psalm 23:4; the Bible's figure for mortal danger and for the darkness through which the shepherd leads)
Hebrew tsalmaveth, deep shadow — traditionally read as tsel, shadow, plus maveth, death, and so rendered by the AV. The word occurs eighteen times, ten of them in Job, and names darkness so thick it is the colour of death.

Biblical Definition

The valley of the shadow of death is walked, not avoided: “Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me” (Psa 23:4). Job uses the word for the grave: “the land of darkness and the shadow of death” (Job 10:21). Isaiah makes it a nation's condition and promises a dawn: “they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined” (Isa 9:2). Zacharias applies that to the Child about to be born: “To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace” (Luk 1:79). And the psalm of the redeemed records the exit: “He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and brake their bands in sunder” (Psa 107:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines shadow, in Scripture, as darkness, obscurity, and the shadow of death as the darkness of the grave, or a state of great danger and distress; and valley as a hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.

VALLEY, n. A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.

SHADOW, n. Darkness; shade; obscurity.

The shadow of death, in Scripture, is used for the darkness of the grave, or for a state of great danger or distress, as of a person about to die.

Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil. Ps. 23.

Key Scripture

Psa 23:4 — "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me."

Job 10:21 — "Before I go whence I shall not return, even to the land of darkness and the shadow of death;"

Isa 9:2 — "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined."

Luk 1:79 — "To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace."

Psa 107:14 — "He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and brake their bands in sunder."

Modern Corruption

The valley is reserved for the deathbed, and the psalm makes it a stretch of ordinary road with the shepherd still walking.

expand to see more

The verse is read at nearly every Christian funeral and the association has narrowed it. The Hebrew word means deep darkness and is used of mines, of the grave, of a nation under judgment, of the eyes of the dying, of a wilderness — any place where a man cannot see the next step. The valley is in the middle of the psalm, between the green pastures and the prepared table, and the sheep goes through it, which means it comes out the other side. It is not the end of the journey; it is the part of the journey in the dark. That widens the verse to cover most of what actually frightens people.

The grammar changes at the valley and the change is the comfort. Verses 1 through 3 speak of the shepherd in the third person — he maketh me, he leadeth me, he restoreth. At verse 4 the psalm turns to address Him directly: thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff. David stops talking about the shepherd and starts talking to Him, and the place he does it is the darkest one in the poem. Many believers could give the same testimony: God was described in the pastures and spoken to in the valley.

Isaiah 9:2 and Luke 1:79 lift the figure from the individual to the world. The people that walked in darkness, that dwelt in the land of the shadow of death, have seen a great light — and Isaiah's next lines are unto us a child is born. Zacharias, holding the forerunner, says the dayspring from on high hath visited us to give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death. The valley of Psalm 23 is finally not a stretch of road one sheep gets through but a condition the whole race sat in, until the Shepherd walked into it Himself and did not come out for three days.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsalmaveth (H6757), deep darkness, shadow of death; gey (H1516), a valley, ravine; choshek (H2822), darkness; Greek skia thanatou (G4639, G2288), shadow of death.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsalmaveth (H6757) — shadow of death, deep darkness; Psalm 23:4, 44:19, 107:10–14, Job 3:5, 10:21–22, Isaiah 9:2, Jeremiah 2:6.

Hebrew gey tsalmaveth (H1516, H6757) — the valley of the shadow of death; Psalm 23:4 only.

Greek skia thanatou (G4639, G2288) — shadow of death; Matthew 4:16, Luke 1:79.

Usage

"“Though I walk through” — through; the road continues."

"“For thou art with me” — the psalm turns from he to thou in the dark."

"“Upon them hath the light shined” — and the next line is a child born."
